TwinkleTwinkle: Interacting with Your Smart Devices by Eye Blink

HAIMING CHENG∗, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong

WEI LOU, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong

YANNI YANG, Shandong University, China

YI-PU CHEN, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong

XINYU ZHANG, University of California San Diego, United States

Recent years have witnessed the rapid boom of mobile devices interweaving with changes the epidemic has made to people’s lives. Though a tremendous amount of novel human-device interaction techniques have been put forward to facilitate various audiences and scenarios, limitations and inconveniences still occur to people having difficulty speaking or using their fingers/hands/arms or wearing masks/glasses/gloves. To fill the gap of such interaction contexts beyond using hands, voice, face, or mouth, in this work, we take the first step to propose a novel Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) system, TwinkleTwinkle, which senses and recognizes eye blink patterns in a contact-free and training-free manner leveraging ultrasound signals on commercial devices. TwinkleTwinkle first applies a phase difference based approach to depicting candidate eye blink motion profiles without removing any noises, followed by modeling intrinsic characteristics of blink motions through adaptive constraints to separate tiny patterns from interferences in conditions where blink habits and involuntary movements vary between individuals. We propose a vote-based approach to get final patterns designed to map with number combinations either self-defined or based on carriers like ASCII code and Morse code to make interaction seamlessly embedded with normal and well-known language systems. We implement TwinkleTwinkle on smartphones with all methods realized in the time domain and conduct extensive evaluations in various settings. Results show that TwinkleTwinkle achieves about 91%9 1 \% accuracy in recognizing 23 blink patterns among different people.

CCS Concepts: •\bullet Human-centered computing Ubiquitous and mobile computing systems and tools; Mobile devices; Interaction techniques.

Additional Key Words and Phrases: eye blink, acoustic sensing, HCI

mobile devices, contact-free user interfaces, including gesture-based, voice input, and silent voice input have been proposed for various contexts. Whereas, there remain limitations that demand urgent solutions to enable interacting with and immersing in environments full of intelligence anytime, anywhere.

Although long considered the primary input method, touching the screen is inconvenient and insensitive when our fingers are busy, wet/oily/dirty, or wearing gloves, even holding the devices in hand. The contact-free HCI method, providing a complementary interaction way, innovates the interaction mode for all-sized devices and presents tremendous potential to the public. Specifically, gesture-based approaches track, recognize, and classify different activities ranging from hand [13, 14, 47, 59, 71, 73] or finger [9, 76, 86] gestures to handwriting [6, 10, 18, 19, 80, 84], vital signs [12, 22, 81, 85], etc., to help users exchange information with devices. Although recent advances have explored different methods to make promising achievements in multiple tracking and recognition applications, many of their usages are constrained by conditions including types of equipment (e.g., hardware or sensor [6, 22]), infrastructure (e.g., Radio-Frequency (RF) systems [85]), line of sight (LOS)/lighting (e.g., camera) and other prerequisites. Besides, on one hand, existing gesture recognition work only identifies a limited number of pre-defined patterns, which yet are not unified but different from system to system and difficult to be remembered. The obvious large-scale hand/finger movement [10, 11, 40, 47, 59, 73, 76, 86] will also incur information leak issues as the content to express behind gestures such as interactive mode, input messages or instructions is evident and easy to be seen, stolen, and mimicked. On the other hand, current gesture-tracking systems are not enough to send commands to devices. More importantly, when people encounter difficulty or inconvenience using their fingers/hands/arms (e.g., loss, injury, or fracture), they can neither perform such gestures nor use a mouse or keyboard. Thus, the gesture-based method still needs further enhancement to promote and apply in life situations considering its accessibility and practicability.

As a natural and convenient interaction modality, the voice-based input approach has been extensively studied and explored owing to the vigorous development of speech recognition technologies. Whereas, vocalizing is not suitable in some quiet places and may face privacy and security concerns in public places [54, 82]. Additionally, speech recognition accuracy may heavily degrade due to ambient noises. To counterbalance the above limitations, recent research on silent voice input is gaining increasing attention. By mapping patterns of users’ lip and tongue motions when speaking silently to the corresponding text [54, 82], silent voice-based interaction approaches can not only assist speech recognition [62] but also serve independently for issuing commands to devices as a non-invasive, privacy-secure HCI mechanism. Some research works that use acoustic signals transmitted by mobile phones to sense lip motions are attracting more and more attention due to better accessibility and mobility [20, 43, 44, 65, 66, 82, 83]. However, each system can only recognize restricted lip motions pre-defined in its own way even leveraging some advanced algorithms, e.g., deep learning. When faced with the epidemic situation where our mouth is covered by a mask, the silent voice input method can not work anymore. Besides, both approaches do not apply to people with speech disabilities [54].

Our approach. Recent years are an intimate depiction of the zone between vigorously developed technologies and the epidemic situation, which entails us thinking about the lifestyle to live with the virus. Based on the need to live in the moment, we ask the following question: Is there an HCI approach that can assist people having difficulty or inconveniences communicating with their hands or mouth to send commands and interact with electronic devices to express themselves? This scenario fuels the interest in researching new methods for enabling communication between people and electronic devices beyond using hands, voice, face, or mouth. Despite that a broad array of HCI techniques and products is emerging, research advances in this field for people are far from being mature.

To remedy this issue, we find that except for hands, mouth, and uncovered face, eyes are the just organ that satisfies all the above requirements, which are always exposed to signals at least a part even wearing glasses, and blinking is a small, quiet and unnoticeable movement, which is suitable for interaction. Although both academia and industry have shown great interest in research on eye blink detection [41], existing advances have different limitations and are not applicable to many scenarios. As a very subtle motion, existing works mainly rely on

Fig. 1. Users hold the smartphone in hand (or employ a stand holder) and blink towards a pair of co-located speakers and microphones in specific rhythms, which will be mapped as commands to interact with the smartphone

cameras [2, 15, 26, 39, 53] or face-attached sensors [17, 31, 55, 64] to detect eye blinking. In addition to light, angle, and LOS requirements, the camera-based approach also suffers from privacy concerns and power-hungry issues, while face-attached sensors are considered uncomfortable and intrusive. Besides, since both cameras and special sensors are costly, such sensors can only be mounted on a small number of devices. What’s more, though high eye blinking detection accuracy can be achieved by these systems, mapping ways between eye blinking and commands are not applicable to support the interaction needs between humans and devices [4, 5, 32, 58] as they either require a display or only provide limited pre-defined commands. To tackle the above problems, we raise the second question: How to design a non-intrusive, accessible, and portable HCI system with the help of blinking, and to make the system recognize patterns not limited to pre-defined ones?

Inspired by the above two desires, in this work, we take the first step to propose an acoustic-based, device-free HCI system, TwinkleTwinkle, which leverages eye blinking patterns as commands to interact with electronic devices through only one pair of mounted mic and speaker. Other than dedicated hardware or wearable sensors, acoustic signals can be transmitted by more and more daily devices, either mobile (e.g., smartphone) or fixed (e.g., TV). Besides, ultrasound signals are not only considered unintrusive but with finer sensing granularity due to shorter wavelength compared with RF signals. Not only to provide an alternative interaction method when on-screen touch is inconvenient and insensitive due to wet, dirty, oily, or gloved fingers but to offer our service to people who have difficulty or inconvenience using their fingers/hands/arms, we deploy TwinkleTwinkle as software on smart devices (i.e., smartphones) so that users can either hold the phone by hand or employ a stand holder to use it in any scenario. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 1, users blink in a specific rhythm towards any pair of co-located speakers and microphones, which emits ultrasound signals and receives eye-blink reflected signals mixed with other interferences. Considering interaction, TwinkleTwinkle depicts eye blink motion profiles and recognizes different blink rhythms as patterns, where blink once as “1”, continuously blink twice as “2”, three consecutive blinks as 𝔰3𝔰^ { \mathfrak { s } } 3 ^ { \mathfrak { s } } , to match them with self-defined commands or existing number combinations like Morse/ASCII codes, thus bridging the interaction barrier from depending on only two blink modalities, open and close, to a variety of one, two, three number combinations and can be embedded with current language systems (not limited to Morse or ASCII codes).

To meet the goal of extracting tiny blink patterns from interferences and designing a brand new mapping relation to renovate traditional pre-defined classification methods, three major challenges need to be addressed.

  1. Detect tiny and aperiodic motions. Recent advances have explored sound signals in different ways to achieve highly accurate motion tracking and recognition. Compared with eye blink motion, these physical activities either have a more apparent scale of displacement (e.g., lip motion [20, 82, 83], handwriting [18, 80]), or their

periodicity (e.g., breathing [70], heartbeats [57, 81]) can contribute to denoising or distracting patterns. Besides, as larger and/or flatter reflectors, they can reflect more signals and yield a higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), while the much smaller and weaker reflection signals of eyelid motions make the eye blink detection task even tougher. A common way to recognize tiny motions [1, 41, 57] is using phases or amplitudes of frequency bins containing such movements in baseband signals of Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW). However, detecting eye blink in this method with acoustic signals needs the help of different textures of eyeball and eyelid to amplify amplitude and periodic head movements to identify frequency bin [41]. Whereas, these two characteristics are not universally applicable to other subtle movements and limit the working range of the sensing device to only facing directly to the eyes or with small deviations.

Towards the constraint, we propose a novel idea to perceive tiny movements without being restricted by the above conditions and no longer need to perform Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and identify frequency bins. Specifically, TwinkleTwinkle employs FMCW and applies a phase difference based approach [13, 14] to depict candidate eye blink motion profiles. This method is not aiming to compete with the frequency bin-based method in terms of accuracy but shows another way to realize and inspire more tiny motion detection works.

  1. Separate blinking patterns from interferences. As an extremely tiny motion, signal variations caused by eyelid displacements are so fragile to be buried by other noises. First, signals reflected by static and moving objects in surrounding environments and direct path signals between the speaker and microphone are received together with the eye blinking signal. Since direct power leakage is orders of magnitude stronger than object reflection due to its shortest propagation distance, a batch of prior works [13, 14, 41, 57, 71] have explored several ways to remove direct power leakage dominated static path interference. Secondly, to make the experimental scenario closer to life, different from previous works [8, 41] that conduct most experiments with the transmitter stationary on the table, a majority of our experiments are conducted by letting testers handhold their phones. In addition, testers have to blink in a controlled rhythm. Thus, except for signals bounced off from surrounding static or moving objects, unconscious movements of the head and hand holding the phone interfere more directly with blink detection. Another phenomenon we found is even if testers try to keep their hands and heads relatively still, the uncontrollable hand and head movements still inevitably exist and can be easily confused with blink patterns as some of them are also subtle, quick, and non-periodic motions. Even worse, the movements are random, uncertain, and vary from person to person. Coupled with the fact we process signals all in the time domain, any tiny differences will show up, which makes denoising and blink recognition even trickier.

To deal with static components, what we find interesting is there is no need to remove static interferences in our system. The rationale behind this is the range of eyelid displacement does not exceed a quarter of ultrasound wavelength (i.e., λ/4)\lambda / 4 ) ). Thus, the phase change of combined signals and blink-induced dynamic components share the same trend. Next, adapted to the phase difference method, we first select phase points less affected by noises and depict candidate blink motion profiles according to three observations. Then, to separate tiny blink patterns from interferences, we model intrinsic characteristics of blink motions through adaptive constraints by analyzing differences between blinks and noises along with similarities and diversities between different people’s blinks. We further distinguish the number of blinks by extracting internal features between each blink. At last, TwinkleTwinkle utilizes a vote-based approach to get final patterns in a sense as a statistical denoising method.

  1. Map blink patterns to number combinations. Existing recognition and classification-based HCI systems typically group activities of a body organ (e.g., hand, lip) into limited categories and map them to different pre-defined commands. However, each system has its own gestures, commands, and map method that are difficult to be remembered or extended. The limitations of the system itself and the lack of commonality between systems hinder the widespread use and practicality of such systems. Since eye blinking only has two modalities, open and close, it is even harder to design an interactive way that sends multiple commands with blinking. Though existing acoustic-based [41] or radar-based [8] work can detect eye blinking, they all stop at further using blinking for interaction. Some video-based approaches need a display and a mounted camera to record the eyes. An eye blink

is similar to pressing the “Enter” button to indicate that a special marker option is selected. Whereas, these systems require dedicated visual interfaces, which makes their use very limited and not easily accessible.

To push the limit of traditional interaction methods, we raise the first pattern design idea: using different blink rhythms, consisting of the single blink, two consecutive blinks, or continuous three blinks to represent patterns composed of numbers *1,2,3*^ { * } 1 , 2 , 3 ^ { * } (e.g., if the pattern length is 1/2/3 digits, 39(=3+32+33)3 9 ( = 3 + 3 ^ { 2 } + 3 ^ { 3 } ) patterns can be formed), then matching them with self-defined commands or existing number combinations like Morse or ASCII codes, especially whose pattern can indicate 26 English alphabets or pinyin. So the system can break the bottleneck of only two blinking modalities to a variety of patterns or be embedded with current language systems. In addition, the proposed rhythm-based interaction design can also solely apply to camera-based or other HCI approaches. To summarize, our main contributions are as follows:

• We take the first step to explore the novel idea of using phase difference of acoustic FMCW signal to sense aperiodic subtle motions such as eye blink in a contact-free way without performing denoising or FFT and no need to resort to different reflection materials and other variations (e.g., breathing) as prior works. The phase difference based approach provides more views to see received signals in the time domain, which can further be applied to detect other tiny movements to benefit and boost more sensing applications.

• We design a new HCI method, which, to our best knowledge, first demonstrates the feasibility of perceiving controlled and rhythmic eye blinking, and mapping different blink rhythms to number combinations for interaction. The rhythm-based number combinations can be not only self-defined for interaction within a system and privacy protection but embedded with a well-known language system for universality and inter-system sharing. The rhythm-based interaction design can not only work solely but apply to and inspire other HCI systems.

• Catering to the rhythm-based blink trajectory profile generated by performing phase difference, we model intrinsic characteristics of eye blink motions through adaptive constraints to separate signal variations associated with eye blink from interferences and distinguish the number of blinks within segmentation.

• We implement TwinkleTwinkle on a smartphone with all methods realized in the time domain and conduct extensive evaluation under various configuration settings and diverse scenarios. The experimental results show that TwinkleTwinkle can recognize 23 different blink patterns from 10 participants with 91%9 1 \% precision in a training-free way, and generalize well across users and environments.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: In section 2, we go over prior arts related to acoustic sensing and eye blink detection. Section 3 introduces the preliminaries of our method to detect tiny and aperiodic motions. Sections 4 and 5 elaborate on the system and technique design of extracting blink patterns from various interferences. Implementation details and experimental results are presented in Section 6. Finally, Sections 7 and 8 discuss and conclude this work.

2 RELATED WORK

2.1 Eye Blink in HCI

Research on the eye blink has long attracted great attention from both academia and industry. Eye blink detection and tracking can serve a wide range of real-life applications, such as eye discomfort detection [17, 23, 24], anti-spoofing [39], attention [16, 31] and fatigue monitoring [15, 30, 33, 55, 64], etc. Especially, eye blink brings up a new HCI method for people with motor or speech disabilities and people whose faces are covered by masks or clothing to communicate with their electronic devices [2, 4, 5, 32, 50, 52, 58]. Existing works mainly prefer to use wearable sensors or cameras to detect eye blinks. Electrooculography (EOG) sensors [31, 55, 64] or proximity [17] sensors are usually mounted on glasses or ears to make their use more convenient and less intrusive. However, devices integrated with these sensors are expensive on the market and may be considered cumbersome and uncomfortable for long time use. Besides, although EOG or proximity sensor-based solutions can get good eye

blinking tracking and detection performance, they more often benefit applications like drowsy drive or attention monitoring but are less for interaction use. Camera-based approaches have been widely explored for a batch of applications [2, 4, 5, 26, 32, 39, 48, 58], not only getting high accuracy in eye blinking detection and tracking but providing a promising way for people, especially those who have motor impaired diseases to interact using their blinks. The proposed approaches usually combine gaze tracking and blink detection, which detect eye blinks to emulate mouse clicks to activate the target application under view [50]. However, camera-based methods always require a display with a camera mounted on to record eye motions, whose interaction scope is limited to the specific developed visual interfaces. Besides, cameras are sensitive to light conditions and LOS scenarios, and the image processing process is power-hungry and computation-intensive.

In contrast, our acoustic-based approach provides a portable, inexpensive, and computation-efficient method for interaction using eye blinking without taking up screen space and is insensitive to shelters, light conditions, and privacy concerns. Though there exists acoustic-based [41] or radar-based [8] work that can detect eye blinking, they all stop at using blinking for interaction. We hope our system may provide a complementary HCI solution to touching-based or vision-based ways.

2.2 Acoustic Sensing in HCI

Due to the convenience and portability of mobile devices along with the finer-grained sensing accuracy of acoustic signals, sound perception drives more refined, mobile, and small-scale moving scenarios compared with wireless signals like Wi-Fi and RFID, ranging from hand [13, 14, 47, 59, 71, 73] or finger [9, 40, 63, 76, 86] tracking and gesture recognition, floor plan [56, 60], traffic safety [28, 29, 38, 79] to keystroke [45, 77] and handwriting inferring [6, 10, 18, 19, 80, 84], lip motion [20, 43, 44, 65, 66, 82, 83], ear canal deformation [7, 21, 74], vital signs like breath [51, 70, 72, 78], heartbeats [57, 81] and lung [61] monitoring, etc. However, current classification-based HCI systems only identify a limited number of pre-defined patterns. Additionally, each work has its own rule of interaction patterns but lacks commonality between systems, which prevents them from being widely accepted. Besides, despite that millimeter-level sensing granularity can be achieved by most of the aforementioned methods, signal variations caused by eye blinking are even smaller and weaker. Previous works sensing extremely subtle motions like heartbeats [1, 57] or eye blink [8, 41] coincidentally prefer to use phase or amplitude in the baseband of demodulated FMCW signals no matter leveraging radar or ultrasound waves. However, the sparsity and aperiodicity of eye blink motion make it even harder to detect blink than heartbeat or breath. The radar-based work can only get blurry patterns with unwanted variations, while the acoustic-based blink detection requires other assistance in identifying blink motions.

2.3 Eye Blink Detection in Acoustic Sensing

There is a recent pioneer work, Blinklistener that applies acoustic FMCW signals for blink detection [41]. It follows the frequency bin-based workflow but creatively addresses the challenges of detecting subtle, aperiodic, and sparse blink motions in the presence of severe interferences from surrounding environments, human targets, and direct power leakage. Specifically, the trajectory of signal variations with both blink and embedded interferences induced by periodic breathing and heartbeat consists of an arc with a “bump”. The embedded interferences cause the arc, while the “bump” is caused by the reflection material switching between eyeballs and eyelids. Blinklistener exploits the embedded interferences to identify the eye-reflection frequency bin and optimal view position that maximizes amplitude variations caused by blink. However, although it is novel to utilize material change of reflection surface and “harmful” interference to boost subtle blink movement, the two features may be not bound with other subtle motions, and the working range of sensing devices is limited once the two conditions are not well satisfied.

Different from Blinklistener, we aim to design an interaction system beyond eye blink detection. Our system proposes a more general way to sense subtle, aperiodic, and sparse movements without leveraging the above

two characteristics owned especially by eye blink, and no need to remove static interferences or perform FFT to identify the frequency bin. It is more sensitive to subtle movements and can work in a broader range, including extremely close contact-free sensing.

3 PRELIMINARY ON SUBTLE MOTION DETECTION

3.1 Signal Design

TwinkleTwinkle leverages a pair of co-located speakers and microphones on mobile devices to transmit and receive inaudible ultrasonic signals carrying signal variations of eyelid motions and employs phase difference-related information in FMCW signals to profile fine-grained eye blink motion trajectories. Here, ?? denotes the number of received FMCW chirps. Based on the baseband signal carrying reflector’s motions, to further extract the subtle eye blink motion-related signal information from the baseband signal, we first briefly introduce the method commonly used in previous works for extremely subtle motion detection, then elaborate on our phase difference-based method.

3.2.1 Prior Methods. To obtain extremely subtle motions like eye blink or heartbeats from received signals in wireless sensing way, prior works, no matter whether based on radar [1, 8] or acoustic signals [41, 57], prefer to leverage phase or amplitude computed at frequency bin corresponding to frequency shift caused by target reflection after performing FFT over baseband signals. Specifically, FMCW signals reflected by reflectors at different distances induce different frequency shifts, which fall into different frequency bins after performing FFT over baseband signals. Without knowing the distance between the reflector and sensing device in advance, there is no way to know which FFT bin corresponds to the measured movements. Prior studies on heartbeats and breathing detection identify the FFT bin corresponding to chest motion by finding the frequency bin with the highest periodicity and largest signal amplitude variation. However, neither of the two methods is applicable to blink recognition as eye blink is a sparse and aperiodic movement with weak and small signal variations. The only study on eye blink detection using ultrasonic signals [41] achieves promising accuracy in virtue of three unique characteristics of eye blinks: different reflection textures between the eyelid and eyeball to get apparent amplitude change; embedded periodic head movements involuntarily caused by breathing and heartbeats to help identify frequency bin related to eyes and optimal view position with maximal amplitude variations. On contrary, our method proposes a more general way for aperiodic and subtle motion detection without performing FFT to identify frequency bins or being restricted by particular features.

So far, we have already been able to obtain coarse eye blink trajectory profiles only by phase subtraction. Next, we will describe why we can see such tiny blink patterns in the presence of all kinds of noises, and how to distinguish nictation from various interferences.

4 SEPARATE BLINKING PATTERNS FROM INTERFERENCES

4.1 Influence of Static Component

We start by analyzing the components of received signals. Signals received at the microphone are the superposition of signals reflected through multiple paths. As illustrated in Fig. 4, the received signal can be considered a combined vector consisting of static and dynamic components. Static components, including signals leaking directly from the speaker to the microphone and signals reflected by static objects, dominate the combined signal since the direct power leakage is orders of magnitude stronger than the other reflections due to the shortest propagation path between the co-located microphone and speaker. The dynamic component, which represents the reflected signals from the moving object, is weaker, especially for eye-blink reflections. Fig. 4 illustrates how the phase of the combined signal changes as the dynamic signal rotates. Specifically, the phase of the static component remains constant, while the dynamic component may rotate 2π2 \pi as the object moves. Since the two components jointly determine the phase of the combined signal, we may observe the combined signal reaches its smallest and

Fig. 6. Trajectories with different similarities

Fig. 7. Relationship between simulated phases and empirical phases

largest phase at the two contact points B and E on the circle with the phase difference β\beta between as its phase change range. Comparing the phase changes of the combined signal with the dynamic component shown in Fig. 4, they neither share the same phase range nor the changing trend. To avoid signal distortion caused by static components, a batch of prior works [13, 14, 41, 57, 71] have explored several ways to remove the static path interference intuitively. Whereas, rather than using the intuitive way of removing the interference of direct path signal, our system extracts the eye blink motion trajectories directly from the combined vector regardless of removing the static interference.

The rationale behind this is, different from other movements, eye blinking incurs a particular small-scale eyelid displacement range. Suppose the eyelid has a thickness of at most 2 mm, resulting in an at most 4 mm distance change in a round-trip, which relates to a repeated phase variation only within a quarter of the ultrasonic wavelength (i.e., 1.7 cm). As Fig. 4 illustrated, since the phase of the dynamic component is always monotonically increasing, it is possible to represent the phase change of the dynamic vector by the combined vector as long as the repeated phase variation does not exactly pass through two tangent points B, E, such as AĈ\widehat { A C } , but falls on the circular for most of the periods where the phase of the combined vector increases or decreases monotonically with the dynamic component (i.e., BDÊ,EAB̂)\widehat { B D E } , \widehat { E A B } ) such as BD̂\widehat { B D } .

To better understand and validate the observations, we further draw the blink trajectories obtained with different phase pairs, which correspond to different phase change intervals of the dynamic component in Fig. 5. Specifically, when the dynamic vector of eye blink rotates repeatedly on BDÊ\widehat { B D E } , the phase change of the dynamic and combined vector share the same trend, which corresponds to the blink profiles shown in Fig. 5(a); when the dynamic vector rotates repeatedly within EAB̂\widehat { E A B } , the phase change of the dynamic and combined vector share an inverse trend, corresponding to the blink profiles shown in Fig. 5(b); when the dynamic vector rotates repeatedly passing points B, E like $\overrightharpoon { A C }$ , the phase of combined signal will experience small up-down variations as shown in Fig. 5(c) and Fig. 5(d). Besides, as the signal strength of the combined signal is stronger than that of the dynamic component, the weak signal variations caused by eye blink will be more apparent by directly using the combined signal. Although there are chances we get eye blink patterns with inverse directions, we are still able to distinguish them from noises. Therefore, we may quantify the correlation by directly using the combined signal phase values rather than the dynamic signal, which is very hard to acquire.

4.2 Select Candidate Trajectories with Fewer Noises

Up to now, we can obtain the eye blink profiles by only selecting phase pairs on the baseband signal for phase subtraction, without time-frequency transform or denoising. However, in addition to the blink trajectory diversity caused by the phase correspondence between the combined and dynamic signals, the irregular and random movements of the head and hand holding the phone seriously aggravate the signal confusion. Since involuntary

movements are inevitable and too uncertain to be regulated or modeled in either time or frequency domain, it is too difficult to guarantee to just obtain a clear blink trajectory every time. To solve this issue, a good feature of the phase difference-based approach is that since two different phases correspond to one trajectory, it provides us with more views to see the received signal in the time domain. As different trajectories contain different noises, if we find several candidate trajectories with fewer noises, there are more chances to get the correct pattern by selecting the most frequent pattern from the candidate lines.

In order to find candidate trajectories that are less affected by interferences, the intuition behind them is to find phase pairs on the phase periods with fewer noises. Towards this idea, we have three observations. First, from Fig. 6, we can observe that blink trajectories with distinct blink patterns have high similarities. Second, we simulate a tiny round-trip movement and compare the simulated baseband signal phase with the empirical one as shown in Fig. 7. Since we choose to use the polyphase filter with the decimation factor of 16 to speed up the filtering process and reduce computational complexity, the output baseband signal will contain 32 samples when inputting a 512-sample signal. The rationale behind the comparison is that the more similar the experimental phase is to the simulated phase, the less noise interference it suffers, as the simulated signal is not affected by noise. Since the phase point with an index smaller than 15 on each chirp may be affected by the low-pass filter, we only compare the phase points with indexes larger than 15. From Fig. 7, what we observe is the phase intervals influenced by fewer noises are more stable and smoother with nearly the same slopes between adjacent phase points, and the phase at the same point on each chirp varies uniformly with time. Conversely, phase points that fall in the black rectangles in Fig. 7(b) will be more likely to correspond to more interference as the phase variations are unstable both within and between chirps. Therefore, the phase pairs we choose would better not fall into the black rectangles. Third, if we use different ϕb(t2)\phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } ) to subtract same ϕb(t1)\phi _ { b } ( t _ { 1 } ) , the resulting lines change more in relation to ϕb(t2)\phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } ) .

Based on the above observations, we develop the following three criteria to select the proper phase intervals in the signal period [(n−1)Ts+τmax,nTs−Tg][ ( n - 1 ) T _ { s } + \tau _ { m a x } , n T _ { s } - T _ { g } ] . Specifically, we first choose fixed-length phase intervals consisting of xx successive phase points in the period [(n−1)Ts+τmax,nTs−Tg]\bigl [ ( n - 1 ) T _ { s } + \tau _ { m a x } , n T _ { s } - T _ { g } \bigr ] . All these xx consecutive points long phase intervals are regarded as candidate phase intervals. In our deployment, xx is set as 5, representing 5 endpoints, which can be denoted as ϕb(t2),ϕb(t2+1),ϕb(t2+2),ϕb(t2+3),ϕb(t2+4).\phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } ) , \phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } + 1 ) , \phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } + 2 ) , \phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } + 3 ) , \phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } + 4 ) . . We set ϕb(t1)\phi _ { b } ( t _ { 1 } ) as ϕb(t2−1)\phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } - 1 ) , and now we have 5 phase pairs. According to the first observation, we measure the similarity between two trajectories using the Euclidean distance and compare the sum of the similarities of all trajectories within each candidate phase interval. We keep three candidate phase intervals with the smallest sum so that we have 15 candidate trajectories. According to the second observation, we measure the stability of one candidate interval by computing the sum of x−1x - 1 variances of slopes between adjacent phase points on all chirps and the sum of differences between the same index phase points on different chirps. We also keep three candidate phase intervals with the smallest sum so that we have 45 candidate trajectories, which is enough for each pattern. If the candidate intervals selected by the three principles are repeated, we change ϕb(t2−1)\phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } - 1 ) to ϕb(t2−2)\phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } - 2 ) or ϕb(t2−3)\phi _ { b } ( t _ { 2 } - 3 ) to avoid candidate phase interval repeat. The reason for keeping three-phase intervals is we find that only keeping one phase interval is not enough or robust due to uncertain signal variations, and since we have to find a most frequent pattern in the end, it is better to keep a single number of phase intervals and candidate trajectories.

4.3 Eye Blink Segmentation and Differentiation on One Trajectory

With the help of candidate trajectories, next, we zoom in on each curve and explain how to segment eye blink patterns in one trajectory along with the way to distinguish different blink rhythms.

At this stage, to extract eye blink patterns from interferences, we usually require profound domain knowledge and deep insight into the features of the target pattern and the differences between blink patterns and interferences. Intuitively, the stereotype of eye blinking is a process of rapid closing and opening of eyelids in a very short time 100∼400ms1 0 0 \sim 4 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m s } ) [41]. Recall that our original intention is to design an interactive way whose beneficiaries

Fig. 8. One user performs eye blinking with the smartphone fixed in a stand holder while keeping the body and head as still as possible with the head against the wall.

can either use it by fixing the transmitter on a stand holder or directly holding the mobile phone. Therefore, different from previous blinking detection works [41] that count numbers of natural blinks with the signal transmitter set on the table, our work takes the first step in perceiving controlled and rhythmic blinking with interferences of uncontrollable hand and head movements of different people. To study signal features of both eye blinking and interference under this scenario, we first let one user perform eye blinking with the smartphone fixed in a stand holder while keeping the body and head as still as possible. Then we invite three users to blink 10 times in any combination of blinking eyes once, twice, or three times in a row. We select representative blink trajectories of different trials as illustrated in Fig. 8 and Fig. 9. With fewer interferences caused by other motions, eye blink movements in Fig. 8 are clearly discernible. Whereas, Fig. 9 demonstrates the individual difference in both blink patterns and the degree of unwanted variations and interferences. From Fig. 9, where red arrows indicate each blink movement and the number of blinks, we could obtain the following findings that we did not know before and are invisible to be identified by only looking at the testers’ blinking. (1) The way of blinking and the degree of natural movements of hands and heads varied between participants. E.g., the three experimenters blink with different durations of eye closure (the tip of each blink motion), user1 being the shortest and user3 being longer, while user2 blinks with severer distorted variations. (2) Different blink trials performed by the same participant are accompanied by different degrees of unwanted variations. As we can see from Fig. 9, the first blink trajectory of each participant is the clearest with the least interferences. (3) The involuntary tremors and blink patterns change irregularly with time through each experiment, and the eye-opening and eye-closing processes are asymmetric. Comparing Fig. 8 and Fig. 9, we can conclude that the involuntary movements of hands and heads are the main disturbances affecting the blink signal. Moreover, the more steady the hand and head (body), the clearer the blink pattern and the easier it is to identify the blink pattern from the trajectory.

Based on the findings above, we are aware of the difficulty that even though it is possible to discern intentional blink movements in multiple modalities of trajectories with naked eyes, it is very challenging to abstract regulations with programs to distinguish where blink patterns are. The extreme value-based peak detection method like LEVD [71] used in previous work [41] may only be workable for blink trajectories containing fewer and less drastic unwanted vibrations such as Fig. 9a(1), 9b(1), 9c(1) and 9𝐜(2){ 9 } \mathbf { c } ( 2 ) . Due to the diversity and uncertainty of both unwanted movements and blinking patterns, it is far from enough to rely only on a fixed preset threshold to measure the difference between local maxima and minima as in prior work [41]. Except for extreme values, finding several features to formulate classification models or using fixed regulations or constraints to decouple segments containing desired blink motions from unwanted vibrations in each trajectory is inappropriate. Due to variances in both blink patterns and interferences of the trajectories, a similar line segment may be part of the blink motion in one blink trial but part of unwanted vibrations in another trial.

To tackle the eye blink segmentation issue regardless of the diversity of both blinks and interferences between people and between each attempt, we are inspired by the way Android and iOS design adaptive user interfaces. Specifically, the adaptive interface can dynamically respond to both internal and external changes by setting relative constraints according to relationships between sibling views and the parent layout, which just suits our

Fig. 9. Representative blink trajectories with coarse segmentation when three users blink 10 times in any combination of blinking eyes once, twice, or three times in a row.

desire that such relative constraints can automatically adjust to match various blink motions with involuntary physical variations in each trial. Based on the above idea, we propose the following heuristic algorithm to find the “edges” that consist of the eye blink induced signal variations.

4.3.1 Coarse Segmentation. We first use coarse constraints to filter out signal variations that are significantly different from the blink-induced patterns. To start with, we cut the trajectory into line segments by alternative local minima and maxima, keeping lines containing more than two sampling points as candidate edges. Since Fig. 9 shows the eye-opening and eye-closing processes are asymmetric, we label the edges starting from the minima and ending at the maxima as the positive direction and vice versa. Then, we filter edges whose length is less than 20%2 0 \% (the discussion on all the threshold settings is included in the last Discussion part of this section) of the longest edge in each direction of each trial, because we find that although lengths of edges that constitute blink patterns vary from trial to trial, their relative lengths to the longest one are deterministic and stable. In addition to longer edge length, we observe that eyelid movement causes rapid changes in at least 3 pairs of sampling points on one edge. So we first compute the difference between adjacent samples on one edge, using the average of the top 3 large difference values as a representative, and remove edges with a representative difference less than 20%2 0 \% of the max difference in each trial. Since we notice that sometimes at the head of some edges appear a cluster of dense points that cannot be counted in eyelid movement time, we trim the start point of each edge to the first sample whose difference from the previous point is larger than 1/4 of the largest difference on the edge. As the blue double arrows shown in Fig. 9a(2), 9b(3), and 9𝐜(2){ 9 } \mathbf { c } ( 2 ) , this trim operation can find a more precise time when the eyelid starts to move, thus helping us better segment each blink. To group the remaining edges into different blink segments, we calculate the time interval between the start points of two adjacent edges and use 0.5 seconds as a time limit. If the time interval between the start point of two edges is less than 0.5𝗌i0 . 5 \ \mathsf { s } _ { \mathrm { i } } , they are classified in the same segment. Once the interval exceeds 0.5 s, the second edge belongs to a new segment.

The segmentation results are shown in Fig. 9 with the orange point as the start and the yellow point as the end of one segment. However, although the above coarse constraints can keep desired blink motions, the results also interfere with unwanted signal variations, which are especially prone to appear near the blink motions as shown in the gray rectangles, or possibly as separate segments as shown in the pink circles. Since we observe that the trajectory varies significantly with time, next, we further apply local adaptive thresholds for finer-grained segmentation based on the current coarse results.

Fig. 10. Results of the fine-grained segmentation

Although the unwanted signals in the gray rectangles or pink circles are very like the right eye blink-induced signal variations, there are still distinguishable features in terms of length and representative difference. For each edge, it has two attributes, the aforementioned edge length, and representative difference, represented as Eij(aij,bij)E _ { i j } ( a _ { i j } , b _ { i j } ) . As Fig. 9 shows, the incorrect segments in pink circles like in Fig. 9b(3), 9c(4) that do not contain any eye blink motions usually have a smaller average edge difference. Therefore, we consider each segment as a group and remove the segment ?? whose average representative difference of aremaining edges, denoted as ∑j=1nibijni\frac { \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n _ { i } } b _ { i j } } { n _ { i } } , is smaller than half the average representative difference of all the rest segments and their inner edges that satisfy the above ∑i=1m∑j=1nibij∑i=1mni\frac { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { n _ { i } } b _ { i j } } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } n _ { i } } constraint, we discuss separately the two cases where there are only two edges and more than two edges composing one segment. Since we observe that the edges that consist of blink patterns either have longer edge lengths or faster sampling point change rates or both, we still use the two attributes, edge length, and representative difference, as constraints in both cases to separate the desired patterns from the unwanted signals. For the situation where a single blink movement induces two edges, we find the length of the two edges is usually symmetric but sometimes closing eyes is much faster than opening eyes. Based on the finding, we determine whether two edges in one segmentation correspond exactly to the eyes’ opening and closing by computing whether the length of two edges is both more than half of the current longest edge or whether the representative difference of either of the two edges is more than 40%4 0 \% of the largest difference of all edges. If either of the two is satisfied, the two candidate edges will be preserved and put in a new set S2S _ { 2 } ; otherwise, they will be discarded. For the case where a segment contains more than two edges, our goal is to remove those unwanted signal variances in the gray rectangles. This time, we use the longest edge and the max representative difference of the segment as reference standards and traverse each edge to see if it meets the criteria. If the representative difference of the edge is larger than half of the local maximum or the length of the edge is larger than half of the local maximum with its representative difference larger than 35%3 5 \% of the local maximum, we keep the edge in the new set S2S _ { 2 } , or else, it will be discarded. The pseudocode for the above fine-grained edge selection process is in Algorithm 1.

end of one segment. We see that our finer-grained segmentation can effectively remove the interferences in gray rectangles and pink circles, and precisely match the eye blink patterns as we want.

4.3.3 Distinguishing Number of Blinks. Since now we get the segments containing eye blink motions, we use the direction of the edges to identify the number of blinks in one segment. We label the edge with a positive direction as “1” and a negative direction as “-1”. If consecutive edges have the same direction, they are recorded only once. For the segments containing one edge, such as in Fig. 9a(2), or one direction (i.e., “1,-1,1-1,-11”), they are considered to blink once. The directions recorded “-11-11”, “1-11-1” or “-11-11-11”, “1-11-11-1” represent two consecutive blinks or three consecutive blinks, respectively. For exceptions with direction records not in the above list, we find that even though the blink patterns share different modalities, a common feature is the points on the edges are sparse but the points on the tips are dense. Therefore, we compute the variance of sample points in the exceptional segment with the window size as 4 and step size of 2 samples, and recognize the number of blinks by counting variance value with shapes of high on both sides and low in the middle.

4.3.4 Over Pruning Correction. Another problem we find is, especially in the case of two or three consecutive blinks, some edges induced by intermediate blinks are mistakenly pruned. As Fig. 10 shows, the remaining edges are deepened in dark gray, but the pink ones are missing, which may result in wrongly recognizing the blink rhythms. Since this phenomenon occurred in all three testers, we guess it may be because people do continuous blinking with weaker eyelid movements in the middle, leading to shorter edge length and intensive sampling point variation that are easy to be filtered out in the fine-grained segmentation part. To get the missing edges back, within the start and end points delineated by the fine segmentation, we add intermediate edges in S1S _ { 1 } but

not in S2S _ { 2 } by checking whether the edge satisfies its length or representative difference is larger than 40%4 0 \% of the second longest edge or half of the second largest difference of the segment. The rationale that we do not add all edges in S1S _ { 1 } within the start and end points is some short, densely sampled edges may still be unwanted lines. The reason why we use the second longest or largest as a reference rather than the first is we need a loose and stable reference than the pruning stage. Using the second one is easier to find adaptive relationships for adding the pink edges back. As shown in Fig. 10, before the correction step, the directions indicated by gray lines in Figs. 10a(3), 10a(4) wrongly represent blink once. After adding the pink lines, the indicated directions represent blink three times, which matches the patterns right. The same cases also can be found in Figs. 10b(3), 10b(4), and 10c(4).

4.3.5 Discussion. Rather than using absolute thresholds or fixed constraints, we set adaptive thresholds to separate blink movements from distorted trajectories, which suits the situation where both desired blink patterns and unwanted interferences vary significantly. All the percentages are empirically set based on the results of data collected from the three users. We first calculate the relative relationship between the attribute of the desired edge and the standard one to determine an approximate range of percentages. And we use 5%5 \% as the step size to find the most appropriate percentages. The results of multiple experiments in Section 6 show that our method can generalize well across users and environments, and can resist different interferences to some degree.

While the above approach yields encouraging results, it is admittedly a heuristic. But the uniqueness of our method lies in that different from other works, we have 45 candidate trajectories for each experiment, which means although our pre-test has 30 experiments in total with 3 testers and 10 trials per person, we actually have 30×453 0 \times 4 5 trajectories as reference for feature extraction, finding relationships and setting parameters. This approach provides us multiple views to see the received signals and results in different situations, which not only helps us gain deep insight into the target pattern to discover unique features but can improve tolerance to threshold setting and interference.

5 VOTE-BASED METHOD FOR FINAL PATTERNS

After processing 45 candidate trajectories through the above segmentation and differentiation procedure, we get 45 candidate blink rhythms. Recall that we apply three criteria to select phase intervals in Section 4 where each criterion corresponds to 15 candidate blink rhythms. We first find the most frequent pattern among every 15 trajectories, then select the one with the highest number of occurrences from the three results as our final rhythm. The reason we do not consider 45 trajectories as a whole is we are afraid the results will interact with each other and lead to the accumulation of wrong patterns as well.

6 IMPLEMENTATION AND EVALUATION

6.1 Implementation

To evaluate the performance of our system, we implement TwinkleTwinkle as an App on the iOS platform. We employ an iPhone SE to control the sending and receiving of ultrasound signals and forward the recorded signals via Wi-Fi to the PC server, which performs signal processing using MATLAB [49] in real-time. We deploy the front-end app based on the acoustic sensing framework LibAS [68]. Without losing generality, since all models of phones on the market have at least one pair of co-located microphones and speakers, the bottom pair and the earpiece pair, our system performs well in both configurations. Therefore, users can pick either of the co-located pair towards their eyes when using our system.

6.2 Evaluation Setup

6.2.1 Data Collection. For the commands used for evaluation, we apply Morse code and ASCII code as carriers for better understanding and validating our idea of using number combinations as an interactive medium. Note that our patterns are not limited to the codes but applicable to any *1,2,3*^ { \ast } { } _ { 1 , 2 , 3 } { } ^ { \ast } number combinations, allowing users to flexibly define their own blink patterns and map them to desired commands. in a controlled way, number combinations of more than 6 digits take a longer time and cause eye fatigue. Since number combinations with less than 6 digits can already represent sufficient commands, we verify the commands whose lengths are from one digit to a maximum of 6 digits. For the Morse code, we take a single eye blink to represent the dot symbol and two consecutive eye blinks to denote the line symbol. While for the ASCII code, a single eye blink means bit $" 0 "$ and two consecutive blinks mean bit “1”. As all the ASCII codes start with the bit *0*^ { * } 0 ^ { * } , we only consider the rest seven-bit sequence of each ASCII code starting from the second one. Besides, when encountering three consecutive bit “1”s, we replace the blinks six times with three consecutive blinks. Based on the above design rules, except for the three cases that use one digit, we carefully select 4 number combinations for the other lengths, thus 23 patterns in total. Fig. 11 shows the selected codes for blink validations, where we avoid long codes containing duplicate short ones.

To do the experiments, we recruited 10 participants from our university. They are from East-Asian with ages ranging from 21 to 32. All of them are students and staff with different degrees (e.g., undergraduate, master, Ph.D.) and diverse backgrounds, including humanities, science, and technology. The participants repeated each pattern 10 times. They completed the experiments on their own schedules (e.g., taking short breaks when feeling eyelid fatigue, conducting the experiments at different time slots or even at different dates).

6.2.2 Experimental Setup. Most of our experiments were conducted in an ordinary meeting room, where there existed various background noises such as server running, air conditioner, and people talking. The measured background noise was around 60 dB (sound pressure). Before the experiments, there was a brief introduction to the participants about the motivation of our work along with the experimental process of data collection. The participants were allowed to have several tries to practice rhythmic blinking and get familiar with the system. For the experiments that required holding the phone in hand, participants were asked to keep their hands and heads as still as possible. Since the participant’s arm might get tired due to the long testing time, they could either keep their arms on the table or not. Participants could choose a comfortable head angle as long as they kept their eyes facing the microphone and speaker, and they usually preferred to hold the phone 15-20 cm away from their eyes.

When designing the experiments of our system, we carefully considered the following points to let our interaction system benefit a wider range of people and contexts. (1) We want to offer our service not only to people who have difficulties using their fingers/hands/arms via the stand holder but to normal people when touching the screen is inconvenient and insensitive due to wet, dirty, oily, or gloved fingers to satisfy mobile and ubiquitous everyday scenarios like holding the device or the mic-speaker is on a smartwatch. (2) Our experiments show that the unwanted signal variations aroused by hand tremors vary from person to person. Thus, to evaluate the effectiveness of our system in tolerating interference caused by different levels of hand tremors, we performed experiments by letting various participants hold the phone in their hands. (3) The voice, silent voice input, or camera-based approach can all work with a device held in hand or fixed on a holder. Based on the above concerns, we conduct experiments with both the phone held in hand and fixed on a holder to demonstrate the validity and applicability of our system in supporting different scenarios. For experiments requiring a phone stand, the phone

After pressing the start button to begin emitting ultrasound signals, the testers need to wait around 1 second for signal synchronization and then start blinking.

6.2.3 Evaluation Metrics. Since we use number combinations to represent patterns, any wrong digit in one pattern means the number combination is wrongly recognized. The accuracy is defined as the number of correct patterns over the total performed number combinations.

6.3 Overall Performance

6.3.1 Hold the Phone in Hand. The performance of TwinkleTwinkle across the 10 participants is presented in Fig. 13(a), showing an average accuracy of 91%9 1 \% when the smartphone is held in hand. Due to variance in both blink movements and interferences of different users, the accuracy of diverse participants ranges between 86%8 6 \% to 99%9 9 \% . Among these testers, User 8 achieved an accuracy of 99%9 9 \% with only 3 errors out of 230 blink trials, which indicates our system can be well accepted and mastered. Besides, although all the users were told to keep their hands and heads as still as possible, involuntary movements were inevitable and differed from person to person. We can tell User 3 and User 8 with accuracy above 95%9 5 \% might have a steady hand and less interfering head movements, while User 2 and User 9 with accuracies of 86%8 6 \% had more uncontrollable jitters. The results shown in Fig. 13(a) can confirm that TwinkleTwinkle is effective with all participants considering user diversities in both blink habits and other physical movements.

6.3.2 Different Code Length. To understand the impact of number length on blink performance, we illustrate the accuracy of patterns with different code lengths in Fig. 13(b). It can be seen that as the code length increases, the detection accuracy gradually decreases from 96%9 6 \% to 87%8 7 \% . The reasons are, on the one hand, we found that testers were more likely to experience eyelid fatigue when they had controlled blinks of more than 5 digits. On the other hand, the longer the code length, the harder it was for the testers to keep their hands and heads relatively still. Therefore, more noisy variations were introduced as the code length got longer, which decreased the accuracy. However, even if we shorten the code length to 4 digits, our system can still recognize 120(=3+32+33+34)1 2 0 ( = 3 + 3 ^ { 2 } + 3 ^ { 3 } + 3 ^ { 4 } ) number combinations with an accuracy of 90%9 0 \% , which is enough for daily use.

6.3.3 Impact of Phone Holder. In order to explore how different levels of hand tremors in different people affect blink accuracy and evaluate the system performance when people can not hold the phone in hand, we asked four people with different accuracies in the above experiment to blink their eyes towards a phone held by a phone holder. The comparison of results under the two situations is shown in Fig. 14. Except for User 7 whose accuracy dropped slightly from 99%9 9 \% to 95%9 5 \% , the detection accuracy for User 1, User 2, and User 5 improved by 8.5%8 . 5 \% , 3%3 \% ,

6.4 Impact Factors

6.4.1 Eye Size. Although it is commonly agreed that a larger eye size can lead to higher accuracy as a larger reflection area makes signal changes induced by the target more apparent, we are curious about the effect of eye size on accuracy in the presence of subtle hand/head movements. As is shown in Fig. 15, we can learn that eye size still dominates the influence, but the unwanted motions carried by different people also affect the effect to a certain extent and make the results more random. The performance is affected by a trade-off between signal variations induced by eye movements and interferences caused by unwanted motions.

6.4.2 Chirp Bandwidth. As elaborated in Section 3, TwinkleTwinkle depicted blink trajectory using phase difference without being limited by the bandwidth of transmitted FMCW signals. To validate the impact of the bandwidth of FMCW on the system accuracy, we evaluated the performance of TwinkleTwinkle with different bandwidths under the situation where testers blinked at the smartphone, which was held in their hand and placed about 15cm1 5 \mathrm { { c m } } from eyes. Specifically, we opted for bandwidths BB with 18−20kHz1 8 { - } 2 0 \mathrm { k H z } , 18-22 kHz, and 17−23kHz1 7 { - } 2 3 \mathrm { k H z } (namely ?? = 2 kHz, 4 kHz, and 6 kHz), since sound waves less than 17kHz1 7 \mathrm { k H z } became audible and intrusive, which hindered the performance of the system and the highest frequency of mobile phone capped at 24kHz2 4 \mathrm { k H z } .

Fig. 16 shows the blink accuracy of our system under different bandwidths, where we can see the accuracy of the transmitted FMCW signal with 6 kHz bandwidth is comparable with the one of 4kHz4 \mathrm { k H z } . Besides, we observe that the accuracy of our method with 2kHz2 \mathrm { k H z } bandwidth slightly drops to 87%8 7 \% . We infer the rationale behind this is the 2kHz-bandwidth FMCW signal is inherently less sensitive to target movements as it can only see objects using a 2kHz2 \mathrm { k H z } narrow bandwidth, which may lead to less effective signal information.

6.4.3 Different Phone Positions and Orientations. Exploring the valid range and angle of the mobile phone relative to the eyes can meet people’s needs in some special scenarios. In this part, as is shown in Fig. 17, we evaluate the robustness of TwinkleTwinkle in terms of distance, height, slope, and angle of the smartphone with respect to the eyes. To minimize other interferences, we conducted the following experiments using a phone holder. The phone was placed about 15∼20cm1 5 { \sim } 2 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } from the testers’ eyes.

Distance. To evaluate the impact of distances between the phone and users’ eyes, we placed the phone towards users’ eyes at different distances of 5∼60cm5 { \sim } 6 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } . As Fig. 18(a) shows, we get relatively good performance with an accuracy of over 90%9 0 \% within 30cm3 0 \mathrm { c m } using the default chirp duration of 480 samples. An interesting phenomenon we observed is that as the eyes gradually move closer to the phone, subtle movements of both eyelids and body are enhanced. Since blink accuracy is determined by the trade-off between desired eyelid movements and unwanted body movements, the accuracy may decrease when users are too close to the phone. However, the system accuracy reduces drastically as distances exceed 30cm3 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } . After extending the transmitted signal period to twice its original length, i.e., 1024 samples/period with the first N=960N = 9 6 0 samples as chirp duration, what we found interesting was accuracies at distances longer than 30cm3 0 \mathrm { \ c m } significantly improved, achieving 92.5%9 2 . 5 \% within 30∼503 0 \sim 5 0 cm and falling to 83%8 3 \% at a distance of 60cm6 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } . We infer the rationale behind this is a longer chirp duration can improve the SNR of reflected signals, which may balance the degrading SNR caused by signal attenuation over distance, thus increasing detection accuracy [35, 41, 47]. Unlikely, further prolonging chirp length will no longer contribute to increasing sensing accuracy on longer distances due to extremely subtle blink displacement and the small reflection area. Yet slower response may particularly degrade the estimation of consecutive two or three blinks.

Overall, as is shown in Fig. 18(a), our system can achieve an interaction accuracy of over 90%9 0 \% within a distance of 50cm5 0 \mathrm { c m } and can even get a good performance of over 90%9 0 \% accuracy at extreme proximity of within 5 cm as shown in Fig. 22(7). Note that frequency bin-based work cannot work at such close distances because high-intensity signals leaking directly from the microphone to the speaker can affect the first few FFT bins corresponding to close range. We believe such a working range is sufficient to support the wide variety of everyday interaction scenarios. Besides, though we improve the sensing performance over longer distances by extending the chirp duration, the limited sensing range has long been a major constraint that prevents the wide adoption of acoustic sensing in real life, which becomes severer for fine-grained activities [36]. We learned a lot from existing advances in solving the sensing distance problem, whose solutions include applying a microphone array [35, 37, 47] and/or advanced deep learning techniques [46, 47], or recent novel methods introducing the idea of a virtual transceiver [36] and moving platform [42]. However, pushing the sensing range limit based on our phase difference-based approach remains a challenging task that we leave as our important future study.

Height. We evaluated the effect of phone height on accuracy by placing the phone at different heights from −15cm- 1 5 \mathrm { c m } to 15cm1 5 \mathrm { { c m } } with a step of 5cm5 \mathrm { { c m } } . As is shown in Fig. 17, we define the height at eye level as 0cm0 \mathrm { c m } . When the phone is under the eyes, the height is recorded as negative while the opposite is positive. We kept the built-in microphone about 15cm1 5 \mathrm { { c m } } away from the eyes during the movement but always faced the horizontal direction instead of the tester’s eyes. The results are shown in Fig. 18(b), although the accuracy decreases as the height difference increases, an interesting phenomenon we observed is that the results are asymmetric. The blink recognition accuracy is higher than 95%9 5 \% with phone height between −10∼5cm^ { - 1 0 \sim 5 } { \mathrm { c m } } and can achieve 80%8 0 \% accuracy when the phone is 15cm1 5 \mathrm { { c m } } below the eyes. Whereas, the accuracy drops to 60%6 0 \% when the phone is moved upward to 10cm1 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } above the eyes. We infer the rationale behind the asymmetric results in two aspects: 1) Due to inherent movements of eyelids, more pronounced changes in eyelid displacements can be observed from below the eyes than from above; 2) When the phone is placed under the eyes towards the body, more body reflections make the collected signals contain more static components. As analyzed in Section 4.1, static components can help to increase the strength of combined signals. Therefore, more apparent blink movements can be captured when the phone is under the eyes.

6.4.4 Different Kinds of Interferences. To further explore the impact of different kinds of interferences, we evaluated the performance of TwinkleTwinkle under three typical kinds of interferences: static interferences, dynamic interferences, and audible noises. As illustrated in Fig. 19(a), we enhance the effect of static interference by having the user sit in front of three monitors. To strengthen the dynamic interference, we let the interferer wave a 12.9-inch iPad near the tester’s eyes quickly and repeatedly when the tester was blinking. Besides, as the noise level of the room where we did experiments was around 60 dB, we chose to test a 70 dB noise environment

The accuracy under different kinds of interferences is shown in Fig. 19(b), which indicates our system is robust to both static interference and audible noises with an accuracy of over 92%9 2 \% but degrades to 87.5%8 7 . 5 \% under intentional dynamic interference. The ability of our system to resist static interference verifies the logic about no need to remove static interference stated in Section 4.1, while the audible sound will not affect our system in that received signals would first pass a high-pass filter to remove audible background noises. However, the intentional dynamic interference is too close to the eyes. Even if its speed and range are different from the eyelids, the reflected signal will still be affected.

6.4.5 Different Postures. To validate how our proposed method behaves when testers use the phone in different postures, we tested TwinkleTwinkle for multiple postures: sitting naturally, sitting with the elbow against the table, standing naturally, and lying. Users held the phone in hand at a comfortable distance (around 15−20cm,1 5 { - } 2 0 ~ \mathrm { c m } , with the top speaker and mic towards the eyes. As results shown in Fig. 20, accuracy is higher when the elbow is on the table or lying down, while accuracy is lower when sitting or standing with the elbow in the air. The results just match our previous analysis, involuntary movements caused by the head and hand holding the phone will affect blink detection accuracy. The more one can keep his/her hands and head relatively still, the better the accuracy is achieved.

6.4.6 Different Daily Environments. To further test the anti-interference capability of our system, we conducted tests in various daily environments, including an ordinary office with many people, several desks, and multiple servers running; a table-dense campus dining hall; outdoor table in windy weather. Users did experiments with the phone held in hand and in the same setting as the above evaluations. We can see results shown in Fig. 21 are all very ideal, which shows the robustness of our system in daily use. This is because the environmental interferences that may occur in daily life can be handled well by our proposed methods.

6.4.7 Impact of Phone Type. To investigate the potential influences of manufacturing and setting variations of speakers and microphones on our system’s performance, in this part, we tested the performance of TwinkleTwinkle with different phone types. These experiments were carried out by testers with mobile phones in their hands. Table 1 lists the sizes and configurations of different mobile phones and the corresponding accuracies. We can see that although the distance between the microphone and speaker varies with the phone size, our system can achieve over 90%9 0 \% accuracy when the microphone and speaker co-locate on the same side. Nevertheless, for the iPad 6, the accuracy reduces to 75%7 5 \% because its microphone and speaker locates at the top and bottom sides, respectively, facing different directions and widely spaced. Since almost all mobile devices now are equipped with microphone-speaker pairs embedded on the same side, we believe our system can be well adapted to different types of mobile phones.

6.5 Case Study

6.5.1 Wearing Glasses, Hats and Masks. In this section, we demonstrate the feasibility of our system in scenarios where people have to wear glasses, hats, and masks. Taking mobile phone authentication as an example, currently, there are few other options besides touch-based and face recognition-based methods. However, in scenarios

(6

Fig. 22. Case study scenarios

where people wear gloves, hats, masks, sunglasses, etc., touch screens and facial recognition are difficult to maintain robustness. The glasses participating in the test are shown in Fig. 22. For glasses shown in Figs. 22(1) and (2), our system can achieve 90%9 0 \% and 85%8 5 \% recognition accuracy when users hold the phone towards the eyes at 10∼15cm1 0 { \sim } 1 5 ~ \mathrm { c m } in front of the face. This is because enough ultrasonic signals can pass through the gap between the two lenses for sensing. However, for the two glasses shown in Figs. 22(3) and (4), our system can only achieve very low accuracy if the phone is still placed in front of the face. It is because the glasses frame is too thick or the glasses lens is too large, only a small gap allows little ultrasonic signals to pass through, whose strength is insufficient to support acoustic sensing.

To improve the accuracy, as is shown in Fig. 22(6), we let the tester keep the bottom of the phone against the nose and glasses so that more signals could reach the eyes and then get reflected. Interestingly, we find both accuracies increase to 90%9 0 \% under this setting since more signals reflected by eyelids would be received and less effect from hand/head tremors would distort the received signals. As far as we know, this is also the first time an acoustic sensing system has demonstrated the ability of such close contact-free sensing. The insight behind is, as our system does not need to remove the direct leakage from the speaker to the microphone, it can sense activities that fall in the same or near frequency bins as the direct path, which can significantly reduce the perception distance. Besides, the situation of wearing a mask and hat is shown in Fig. 22(5) with an accuracy of 95%9 5 \% . We further tested a case with all faces covered as illustrated in Fig. 22(7), getting 92%9 2 \% blink detection accuracy. We envision that our system can not only provide an advanced solution for people wearing masks, sunglasses, hats, and gloves to compensate for the inapplicability of visual and touching-based methods but also be embedded in interactive devices such as smart glasses or headgear to provide proximity interaction.

6.5.2 Inputting Commands. In this part, we show our study on the test of inputting a command such as “open the door”. We first represented each letter of the command in Morse code, thus the command can be decoded as ∞3⊔1221⊔1⊔21⊔2⊔1111⊔1⊔211⊔3⊔3⊔121∞^ { \infty } 3 \sqcup 1 2 2 1 \sqcup 1 \sqcup 2 1 \sqcup 2 \sqcup 1 1 1 1 \sqcup 1 \sqcup 2 1 1 \sqcup 3 \sqcup 3 \sqcup 1 2 1 ^ { \infty } , where 𝔰⊔𝔰^ { \mathfrak { s } } \sqcup ^ { \mathfrak { s } } is used to separate the codes of two adjacent letters. Then we invited three testers to blink the code sequence 5 times following the code’s rhythm with a distinguishable time gap of nearly 1 second between two adjacent letters. However, the average time for inputting the command is approximately 31.5s3 1 . 5 \ s , which is considered time-consuming. Besides, after completing the test, two of the participants reported feeling some eye fatigue during the first 2∼3 rounds due to the unfamiliarity with the system and the tension in the eye muscles. After getting used to the blinking method, blinking in their natural way did not cause much fatigue. The third tester thought blinking in the usual relaxed manner would not feel fatiguing to complete the interaction.

Based on the above observation, although our rhythm-based interaction design can be applied to existing language systems such as Morse or ASCII codes for universality and inter-system sharing, it may be considered cumbersome and time-consuming when inputting long commands. Under this situation, we would suggest users set their self-defined blink patterns for inputting such commands, as our system has the unique feature of allowing
