6.6 HCI-related Issues

6.6.1 User Survey. We conducted two user surveys to investigate the 10 testers’ feedback on our system. The first survey is the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) [25] questionnaire to rate our method’s perceived workload across six dimensions. We also conducted a user study survey to get the subjective reactions of the 10 users regarding the system. As is shown in Table 2, the user study survey includes five questions, focusing on (1) their acceptability of our interaction design motivation (Q1 and Q2), (2) their attitude toward our rhythm-based eye blink idea (Q3), (3) the level of eye fatigue while doing the experiments (Q4), and (4) their acceptability of using the system (Q5). The users were asked to score their answers according to the survey score criteria in Table 3.

The results of the two surveys are shown in Fig. 23. Fig. 23(a) shows the NASA-TLX score of our system from the 10 participants. As the NASA-TLX score ranges from low (1) to high (20), we can infer that users did not need to take much effort when using our system since the average scores of the six dimensions are all less than 10.

Fig. 23(b) demonstrates the percentage of 1∼51 { \sim } 5 points that occurs in each question. We are glad to see that users overall showed positive attitudes toward our system. Nearly 80%8 0 \% of the testers would consider using blinking for interaction when their hands were inconvenient, and 90%9 0 \% of them liked our idea. Most of them could blink for more than 30 minutes before they felt eye fatigue. All users prefer to define their own patterns when possible.

6.6.2 Learnability and Memorability. In order to evaluate the learnability [3, 27, 69] and memorability [67, 75] of our system in mapping blink patterns to their meaning, we considered an application scenario where users use blink patterns to control the phone’s camera in the circumstance that their fingers are inconvenient to touch the screen. For this scenario, we define 6 blink patterns and their corresponding command meanings: (1) We use the pattern *123*^ { * } 1 2 3 ^ { * } to unlock the phone when a user takes out the phone for use. (2) We then use patterns *2*^ { * } 2 ^ { * } and 𝔰22𝔰^ { \mathfrak { s } } 2 2 ^ { \mathfrak { s } } to start and end the photo app. (3) We also use patterns “1”, 𝔰12𝔰^ { \mathfrak { s } } 1 2 ^ { \mathfrak { s } } , and 𝔰21𝔰^ { \mathfrak { s } } 2 1 ^ { \mathfrak { s } } to support three simple actions: press the shutter button, zoom in and zoom out.

We had five testers carry out this experiment. We first introduced the 6 patterns and their corresponding meanings to the testers. Then, we demonstrated how to blink the patterns *1,2,3*^ { * } { } _ { 1 , 2 , 3 } { } ^ { * } . The testers had practiced for three minutes before actual testing. The testers could try 5 times. One tester succeeded on the second attempt, two testers succeeded on the third attempt, and the last two testers succeeded on the fourth attempt. All testers completed their first learning within 15∼201 5 { \sim } 2 0 minutes. The results demonstrate good learnability of our system. To test the memorability, we asked 4 testers to repeat the blink patterns after one day and a week. However, they forgot the patterns in the first trial after one week and had to relearn them. We believe this is due to the facts that the testers did not use these patterns in their daily lives and that they did not define them themselves. Thus, focusing on making the blink patterns and related commands more memorable, we suggest to let users customize their own pattern-to-command mappings or provide additional visual cues such as icons or symbols, through which the users can intuitively make logical and familiar associations to make the pattern-to-command mappings more memorable.

6.6.3 Efficiency. In our system, the average time for blink patterns containing 1/2/3/ 4 bits is 1.1/2.1/3.2/4.11 . 1 / 2 . 1 / 3 . 2 / 4 . 1 seconds, respectively. Compared with the gesture-based system, where it usually takes 1∼2 s to finish a gesture, and the voice-based system, which has the advantage of launching long commands, our system seems to have no obvious advantages in terms of throughput and efficiency. However, the advantages of our system lie in that, we can provide one more interaction alternative when people have difficulty and inconvenience speaking or using their fingers/hands/arms or wearing masks/glasses/gloves. Our system can also provide self-defined patterns as shortcuts for frequently used long commands and perform close contact-free sensing.

7 DISCUSSION

7.1 Comparison with Frequency Bin-based Work

We implemented the other acoustic-based blink detection work Blinklistener [41] on the iOS platform leveraging the frequency bin-based method. Specifically, Blinklistener first performs FFT over the mixed signals obtained by multiplying received FMCW signals with the conjugation of transmitted signals. Then it identifies the frequency bin corresponding to the eye blink by picking up the one with maximum I-Q space signal variations. Finally, it detects blink-induced amplitude changes caused by different reflection textures by finding the optimal viewing position. Despite its promising accuracy in blink tracking and detection, the two systems differ in the following aspects.

  1. The design intention is different. Blinklistener is a blink tracking system, while our system focuses on providing a new interaction method. (2) Besides, regarding the signal processing method, when using the frequency bin-based method for subtle motion sensing, the challenges of such work usually lie in identifying the correct FFT bin and extracting the subtle motion from various interferences. To address the challenges, Blinklistener exploits the embedded interferences induced by periodic breathing and heartbeat to identify the

eye-reflection frequency bin and optimal view position that maximizes amplitude variations caused by blink. The method also needs the help of different textures of eyeballs and eyelids to amplify amplitude. However, although it is novel to utilize material change of reflection surface and “harmful” interference to boost subtle blink movement, the two features may not be bound with other subtle motions. For our phase difference-based approach, it does not need to face the above two challenges. Our system proposes a more general way to sense subtle, aperiodic, and sparse movements without removing any interferences and performing FFT but by trying to find desired signal variations from the received signals and performing all the processing methods in the time domain. The phase difference-based approach provides more views to see received signals in the time domain, which can further be applied to detect other tiny movements to benefit and boost more sensing applications. (3) Furthermore, Blinklistener only achieves over 90%9 0 \% accuracy within a strict sensing device working range, where the effective sensing angular range is ±15\pm 1 5 degrees in the horizontal plane and ±10\pm 1 0 degrees in the vertical plane, and the height range is within ±5cm\pm 5 \mathrm { { c m } } . We infer the reason is that since it requires different reflection textures to get apparent amplitude changes when the orientation of the sensing device deviates from just facing the users’ eyes, the received signal hardly satisfies the requirement, leading to performance decreases. Additionally, Blinklistener can not sense reflectors within about 9 cm of the speaker as they will fall into the same or adjacent frequency bin of the direct leakage and will be overwhelmed by it. Whereas, TwinkleTwinkle achieves over 90%9 0 \% accuracy within a broader device working range. Specifically, the effective sensing angular range is ±30\pm 3 0 degrees in the horizontal plane and −60o∼30o- 6 0 ^ { o } { \sim } 3 0 ^ { o } in the vertical plane, the height range is between -10 to 5 cm. We infer the reason is that since TwinkleTwinkle tries to see the subtle displacement from different aspects in the time domain, it is more sensitive to subtle movements as long as signals can reach the object. Moreover, our system can perform extremely close contact-free sensing as it does not need to remove the direct leakage from the speaker to the microphone so that it can sense activities that fall in the same or near frequency bins as the direct path.

7.2 Comparison with Camera-based Work

Although the camera-based approach may get higher accuracy for capturing eye blinking under such spacial constraints, we position our system as a complementary or alternative method compared to the camera-based systems considering the following aspects. (1) The performance of the camera-based approach degrades in poor lighting situations and is limited by angle ±45\pm 4 5 degrees) and LOS requirements. For the case shown in Fig. 22(5), face recognition does not work, while our system can achieve 95%9 5 \% accuracy. (2) Since the camera sensor is costly, only a small number of devices have a camera mounted. (3) The camera-based approach usually requires an extra window interface to display the user’s face, which may greatly affect the display space. (4) As face recognition may raise power-hungry and privacy concerns, it is commonly used for one-take authentication instead of sending commands for interaction usage. Conversely, our acoustic-based system can be adopted by more devices and contexts as it is cheap, space-saving, power-saving, and privacy-preserving. In addition to working independently, our system can work in parallel with vision-based systems such as embedding on VR/AR glasses or wearable devices because it does not require a screen display and is computationally efficient. We believe there is no cure-all solution. Our system may provide one more interaction option for users when faced with diverse application requirements.

7.3 Limitations and Future Work

7.3.1 Heuristic Setting Adaptive Constraints. In order to segment and differentiate eye blinks on one trajectory, despite we can get barely good results with 10 people based on a heuristic setting adaptive constraints method, whereas, if more people or more unexpected involuntary hand, head, and body movements are involved, or under more dynamic scenarios with variable blink patterns, the performance of our system may decrease. Although there exist many advanced methods to solve picture-based classification problems, seldom can be found for one-dimensional (1D) signals’ tracking and denoising. This raises new changes for us to explore using a more intelligent and automatic method to solve the 1D tracking problem.

7.3.2 Simultaneous Large-scale Movement. Through our experiments, we found that our system cannot detect blinking with user’s head moving or rotating, or in unstable moving vehicles. Specifically, the large-scale and vigorous head moving or rotating will severely disturb or overwhelm signal variations induced by small-scale and weak blink displacement. Therefore, our system requires the users and the phone to stay stationary or keep quasi-stationary for better performance. We find the frequency bin-based work also faces this problem [36]. Therefore, detecting subtle movements buried in other large-scale motions remains a significant yet challenging problem that deserves further research.

8 CONCLUSION

To benefit people with difficulty speaking or using their fingers/hands/arms or wearing masks/glasses/gloves, in this paper, we propose a novel HCI system, TwinkleTwinkle, which senses and recognizes eye blink patterns in a contact-free and training-free manner leveraging ultrasound signals on commercial devices. TwinkleTwinkle first applies a phase difference based approach to depicting candidate eye blink motion profiles, followed by modeling intrinsic characteristics of blink motions through adaptive constraints to separate tiny patterns from interferences. We propose a vote-based approach to get final patterns designed to map with number combinations either self-defined or based on carriers like ASCII code and Morse code to make interaction seamlessly embedded with normal language systems. We implement TwinkleTwinkle on smartphones and conduct extensive evaluations in various settings to demonstrate the effectiveness of our system. The phase difference based approach provides more views to see received signals in the time domain, which can further be applied to detect other tiny movements to benefit and boost more sensing applications. The rhythm-based interaction design can not only work solely but apply to and inspire other HCI systems.
